newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Pol Pot fighters desert - Cambodian premier.
newsitem.headline: Pol Pot fighters desert - Cambodian premier.

text.p: Most of Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot's remaining fighters have deserted him but the reviled leader escaped towards the Thai border with other top figures in the collapsing Maoist movement, a Cambodian leader said on Monday.

About 95 percent of the hardline Khmer Rouge from the movement's camp at Anlong Veng and from Pol Pot's own division, including four unnamed top officials, have decided to join the Cambodian government on June 18, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters.
"This is the end of the Khmer Rouge...," Ranariddh said at a pagoda inauguration west of Phnom Penh. "You are watchers of history...in this country."

Pol Pot, mastermind of the 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror, was reported on Friday to have fled his northwest stronghold of Anlong Veng after the guerrilla movement, its military might already crumbling, split over whether to make peace with Phnom Penh.
Ranariddh said Pol Pot was on the run after slaughtering his defence chief Son Sen and 11 of his family members and still held top comrades as hostages.
Pol Pot fled north on Sunday in a convoy of 10 trucks, but six were caught by rebels who had broken from his own army, Ranariddh said.

Pol Pot was still holding senior figures as hostages, including the president of the Khmer Rouge provisional government, Khieu Samphan. But rebel commander Ta Mok has broken with Pol Pot and disappeared, he said.
Pol Pot was last placed about 25 km (15) miles east of Anlong Veng, where he was thought to have been surrounded by 1,000 rebels from his own army.
"Pol Pot is very isolated, very alone...The rest of the Khmer Rouge will be dismantled very, very soon," Ranariddh said.
He said rebel defectors had seen Pol Pot alive but he was very ill and "in bad shape".
"He is alive, you will see. I hope (we) will be able to capture him," he said, adding he hoped Pol Pot could be brought before an international tribunal for his crimes.
More than one million Cambodians died of starvation, execution, disease and hard labour during the Khmer Rouge rule.
Ranariddh said there was little fighting between the rebels because the breakaway guerrillas "are very cautious about the presence of Khieu Samphan with Pol Pot".
He said Khieu Samphan was still a hostage, a report analysts viewed with scepticism because of his long and loyal ties with Pol Pot.

In a surprise revelation, Ranariddh told reporters he had met Khieu Samphan and two of his associates three weeks ago in Preah Vihear, a rebel base about 50 km (30 miles) east of Anlong Veng, to broker peace.
He refused to provide details of the meeting, which he said was rendered meaningless by subsequent events.
Ranariddh said Pol Pot's right-hand man Nuon Chea was also a hostage.
Among those who escaped with Pol Pot were Chan Youran, Pech Bun Reth, Chun Cheoun, Tep Khunnal, Kao Bun Heng and Mok Ben, who are senior officials in the guerrilla movement.
The Khmer Rouge, which reneged on a 1991 peace pact meant to end Cambodia's long history of conflict, has been fighting the coalition government formed following U.N. polls in 1993.
But it has been decimated by thousands of defections since last August.
